title: Glad at your going
hookLine: no one is so lucky that no one will be glad at their death, not even Marcus (Meditations 10.36)

lines: THE LAST DAY AT A JOB.
cards: The last day at a job: the cake, the card, the kind speeches. And somewhere in the room, someone quietly relieved you're going. Maybe you never knew, and maybe that was for the best.
Marcus, emperor of Rome, writes in book ten that it would be the same at his own death: someone standing by would be glad. Not because he was cruel. Just because that's how people are.

teach.b: First, the claim. No one is so fortunate, Marcus writes, that when they're dying there won't be some standing by who welcome what's happening.
Second, even the good. Suppose the person was good and wise. Won't someone still say under their breath: at last we can breathe again, free of this schoolmaster?
He was never harsh with any of us, but I always felt him quietly judging us. That, Marcus says, is what's said of a good man. Third, and me?
Then he turns it on himself.

In my case, he says, there are many more reasons people would be glad to be rid of me. Even the companions he has worked for, prayed for and cared for will want him gone, hoping to gain something by it.
Humbling words, from a man who ruled the Roman world. Fourth, how to hold it. Not with bitterness.
Don't, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them, Marcus says. Keep your own character: friendly, well-meaning, gentle. Let go easily, not as if you were being torn away.
So the thought is a lightness, not a wound. If even the gentle schoolmaster can be resented, anyone can.
You aren't the center of everyone's world, and that's a kind of relief.
Hold your importance lightly, and keep being kind.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this passage to loosen the sense of being indispensable, picturing life going on without them while resolving to stay kind to everyone around them.

o: a good man someone is quietly relieved to see go
a strict teacher who punished his pupils harshly
a tutor Marcus hired to teach his own children

games.q: glad at your going — tap the pairs.
p: what the good man is called

s: Marcus assumed everyone would mourn a good emperor
he writes that no one is so fortunate that some won't be glad at their death, himself included.
he says not to leave with less kindness toward them because of it
keep your own character, he writes: friendly, well-meaning, gentle.

games.q: you learn someone will be relieved when you leave. you're Marcus. how do you go?
o: as kind as ever, holding your importance lightly.
games.why: don't go away less kindly disposed toward them, he writes; keep being friendly, well-meaning and gentle, and let go easily.

practice: Think of one place where you feel important, a team, a family, a group of friends, and let yourself picture it going on without you: someone else running the meeting, a family dinner with your chair empty.
Notice whatever comes, a sting or something lighter, and breathe out a little of that weight. Then picture going back in, as kind as ever.

wordCard.voice: Schoolmaster. Marcus imagines himself as the schoolmaster someone will feel relieved to see go, even though he was never harsh. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the household slave who walked a child to school and kept watch over him. Marcus imagines being called one.

carryVoice: Your line: lightly. Not everything, and not everyone, rests on you. Day six hundred twenty, done.
